summary: TrustFlame is an AI fire-safety assistant that checks itself. It reads all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's PSI database and 2,001 test rows, then summarises, ranks and interprets them for five crew environments: space station, spacecraft, Moon base, rover and Mars base. Its answers come only from NASA sources, and a claim-level guardrail checks every sentence and every number against the evidence before anything is shown; when the evidence is not there, it declines instead of guessing. We tested it the way a scientist would: 22 questions written by our team from the challenge resources, 18 passed, and every result, including the failures, is published on the site. The 42 NASA quotes that link research to equipment are verified word for word by the code. The result is a real finding: no real solid sample in NASA's tables was tested above 22.2% oxygen, while a Moon base is expected at 30% or more. It works in Arabic and English, fully offline, at no cost.
details:
Detailed Project Description

What it does. TrustFlame turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight through seven pages:

Story: the case told by scrolling, with real ISS flame video and NASA's own words on Apollo 1 and Mir.

Investigations: all 24 PSI combustion investigations ranked 0 to 100 for a chosen crew environment, with filters and full details.

Moon readiness: choose an oxygen level and a pressure, and see how many NASA tests reached those conditions, with which materials, and what happened to the flame.

Research to equipment: which investigations inform smoke detectors, suppression, ventilation, material selection and fire models. Every link quotes NASA word for word.

Test data: every PSI test table plotted, with normalised columns and CSV export for modelling.

Ask: questions in Arabic or English, answered from NASA passages only and checked sentence by sentence.

Overview: key findings and the oxygen range of every investigation.

How it works. Download scripts collect the PSI investigation records, their experimental tables and every resource on the challenge's Resources tab. A build step normalises the tables (oxygen, pressure, flow, fuel names, flame outcomes), corrects known errors inside the source files and reports them as data notes, and produces 475 knowledge passages. For a question, hybrid retrieval (meaning plus exact words) selects the passages, a local Llama 3.2 model drafts an answer from them only, and a guardrail compares each sentence with the evidence and requires every number to appear in it. Unsupported sentences are removed in front of the user; if too little is supported, the system declines. Arabic answers are translated sentence by sentence and re-checked for numbers and names.

Benefits. An engineer choosing materials for a Moon base sees in seconds what NASA tested and what it did not. Arabic-speaking students and researchers can read NASA combustion science in their own language. Because the tool counts real tests instead of predicting risk, it shows data gaps honestly: no solid material was tested at the expected Moon base atmosphere.

Validation. Every quote on the site (42 research-to-equipment quotes and the story quotes) is checked word for word against its NASA source, and the build stops if one is not found. The assistant was tested on 22 questions written by team members from the challenge resources (20 to answer, 2 to decline): 18 passed (82%), and every result is shown on the site. One failure shows a real limit we report: asked about the 1997 Mir fire, the model added that a flame burned for over 45 minutes, a fact from a different Mir experiment; the number check passed because 45 does appear in the retrieved evidence. Checking each number against the right passage is our next improvement.

Limits. An answer takes 1 to 2 minutes on a laptop CPU. The check uses meaning similarity plus number matching, not a trained entailment model. The checked answer is English; its Arabic translation comes from a small model and can be wrong in meaning, so it is shown under the English text and labelled as approximate. PSI has no partial-gravity data yet, so the tool does not predict lunar-gravity behaviour.

What we hope to achieve. A trustworthy front door to NASA's combustion data: add the lunar-gravity experiments NASA expects to publish (LUCI, FM2), a stronger Arabic model, and analysis of the raw video archive.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Requests, PyMuPDF), JavaScript, HTML and CSS without a framework, Ollama running Llama 3.2 3B and bge-m3 locally, Git and GitHub. Open source under Apache-2.0.
